title: The Great Space Station Sock Chase

topics.value_lesson: The crew succeeds because each person's small job holds up everyone else's big job — teamwork as the real spacesuit

spine: A new crew of astronauts turns their first day on the space station into an escalating game of catch, learning that teamwork holds them together even when everything else floats apart.

segments.text:
We are the newest crew on the space station, and today we get our first real job. Yesterday we were still in the underwater training pool, where Coach Dex taught us to tighten bolts while floating upside down. "Slow hands," Coach Dex burbled through the water. "Space likes slow hands."

Now Commander Rosa floats beside us in the kitchen corner, with her boots hooked under a rail so she does not drift away. "Crew," she says, "unpack the kitchen. Make it ours."

We unzip the lunch pouch. We are careful. We are so careful.

But out pops a pea.

It does not fall. Down here, nothing falls. The pea just floats, slow and green and serious, right past Commander Rosa's ear.

"Oh," says Commander Rosa.

The pea bumps the window and turns, like a tiny green moon that forgot where moons go.

Then the speaker crackles. "Station, this is mission control." It is Flight Director Bea, and we can hear her smile. "You have a visitor up there."

Commander Rosa looks at us. We look at the pea. The pea looks at nobody, because it is a pea.

"Crew," says Commander Rosa, "what do we call him?"

"Chase it!" we shout, because we cannot help it.

The pea bobs past the sleeping bags, which are stuck to the ceiling like bats in pyjamas. We push off after it.

Here is the secret nobody told us: there is no up and no down here. The ceiling is a floor if you want it to be. We bounce. We tumble. We bump the wall with our knees and laugh.

"Wait," says Commander Rosa, unhooking her boots. "New game. Catch General Pea without touching any wall."

We reach. The pea drifts. We stretch out one long arm, and the pea turns, slow and green and serious, just past our fingertips.

"He is winning," says Commander Rosa, bumping the ceiling with her head. "He has trained for this."

The speaker crackles. "Station, how is the visitor?" asks Flight Director Bea.

"Undefeated," says Commander Rosa. "Mission control, why does juice climb straws?"

"Ask Coach Dex," says Bea. "And crew? He says: slow hands."

Slow hands. We stop reaching. We wait. The pea floats closer, closer —

and bumps our open palm like it meant to all along.

"Gotcha," we whisper.

"Now," says Commander Rosa, grinning, "who wants to let him go again?"

"Let him go," we say. "He has places to be."

General Pea drifts toward the window, slow and green and serious, like a tiny moon on important business.

The speaker crackles. "Station, this is mission control." It is Coach Dex this time, and we can hear the training pool in his voice. "If you want a real game, start bigger. One sock. Slow hands."

One sock. We toss it. It turns over and over like a sleepy fish, and Commander Rosa catches it against her chest.

"Too easy," she says. "Next."

A shoe. Then two socks. Then — somebody shouts it — the commander's lunchbox.

"My lunchbox," says Commander Rosa, delighted. "Fine. But if we lose it, we eat toothpaste for dinner."

The lunchbox sails. Three of us bounce off the walls to intercept it, and Commander Rosa hooks her boots under the rail and leans out like a goalkeeper.

"Mine!" we shout.

"Mine!" she shouts back.

The lunchbox spins past us all, heading for the kitchen wall — the Velcro wall, where everything sticks to everything and spoons go to be lost forever.

"Oh no," says Commander Rosa. "My pudding is in there."

Back in the kitchen corner, the pea is still floating, slow and green and serious. But now it has company. A wobbly ball of orange juice is drifting right beside it, and both of them are heading for the control panel.

"Oh no," says Commander Rosa. "My lunchbox!"

But it is too late. The lunchbox bumps a switch. The juice ball bumps another. And suddenly the whole station is playing music — loud, bouncy, terrible music.

"My playlist!" says Commander Rosa. "Isn't it wonderful?"

It is not wonderful. But Coach Dex's voice crackles over the speaker. "Crew, time for your two hours of space exercise!"

"Can we exercise to the music?" we ask.

"Slow hands," says Coach Dex, "but fast feet!"

So we dance. We bounce off the walls. We spin like slow tops. The pea bobs past us, and we could swear it is dancing too.

Then the Velcro chaos begins. The checklist sticks to the sock. The sock sticks to Commander Rosa. And Commander Rosa sticks to the wall.

"Crew," she says, wiggling one boot, "I appear to be stuck."

The music plays on. The pea floats by, looking very pleased with itself.

"A chain!" says Commander Rosa. "Pass me down, one hand at a time."

So we build a chain of us. I grab the rail. You grab my ankle. The next hand grabs yours. We stretch down the module, wobbling like a slow banner, and the last hand grabs Commander Rosa's boot.

"Pull!" we shout.

We pass her along, hand over hand, and every small handhold matters. My job is just to hold on. But my holding holds you, and your holding holds her. Rip! The Velcro lets go, and the whole chain sproings into a giggling knot.

"Crew," says Commander Rosa, peeling a sock off her shoulder, "that is exactly how a crew works."

Then she goes quiet. "Look."

Outside the window, the Earth is sliding into its ninth sunrise of the day. And there hangs the Moon, close and bright and round.

"Some crews are training right now," she says softly, "to walk on that."

We press our noses to the glass. Behind us, the pea bumps gently against the window, turning slow and green and serious.

"He wants to be a moon too," we say.

So we tuck him into a pouch, safe and snug, our very own tiny green moon to take home.

"Slow hands," says Commander Rosa, smiling. "Good work, crew."

"A race!" says Commander Rosa, wiggling her stuck boot. "Far end of the station. No touching anything. And the winner is whoever crashes the softest."

"You're stuck," we point out.

"Then you'd better crash into me very, very softly."

We push off. We float. No hands, no feet, just us drifting down the whole long module like slow dandelion fluff. The terrible music plays. The pea bobs alongside us, racing too, in its solemn pea way.

"Don't touch the walls!" calls Commander Rosa.

Too late. You bonk a rail. I spin like a top. We are not winning on style.

But ahead of us, the sleeping bags wait, fat and puffy and strapped to the wall right beside the commander. We aim for the softest one. We tuck. We land.

Floof.

It is the softest crash in the history of crashing. The whole wall of sleeping bags puffs out, and the Velcro lets go with a happy rip, and Commander Rosa tumbles into the pile with us, laughing so hard she can't talk.

The speaker crackles. "Station, this is mission control." Flight Director Bea is laughing too. "We've been watching. You are officially the silliest crew in orbit."

We unstrap a Moon dust sticker from the care package and press it on our sleeve. And past the window, slow and green and serious, General Pea sails on, orbiting his station, keeping an eye on his crew.

gathered_but_unused: Astronauts train underwater in a giant pool because floating in water feels a lot like floating in space.
There is no up or down in space, so astronauts sleep strapped to walls, ceilings, wherever there's room.
In orbit, a dropped spoon doesn't fall — it just hangs in the air waiting for you to come back.
Astronauts' food has to be sticky or in pouches, because crumbs float into noses and equipment.
On the space station, the sun rises and sets sixteen times every single day.
Weightlessness makes astronauts' spines stretch, so they come home a few centimetres taller for a little while.
Mission control is a room full of people on the ground whose whole job is helping the crew do theirs.
Astronauts exercise about two hours a day in space, or their muscles get lazy in weightlessness.
